<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" title="In A.1 Dataset Set-Up ‣ Appendix A Experimental Set-Up ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Places-365 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<span class="ltx_ref">32</span>)</cite>.</span></a></li>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">In many retrieval systems the original high dimensional data (e.g., images) is mapped to a lower dimensional feature through a learned embedding model. The task of retrieving the most similar data from a gallery set to a given query data is performed through a similarity comparison on features. When the embedding model is updated, it might produce features that are not comparable/compatible with features already in the gallery computed with the old model. Subsequently, all features in the gallery need to be re-computed using the new embedding model – a computationally expensive process called <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">backfilling</em>.
Recently, compatible representation learning methods have been proposed to avoid backfilling. Despite their relative success, there is an inherent trade-off between the new model performance and its compatibility with the old model.
In this work, we introduce FastFill: a compatible model update process using feature alignment and policy based partial backfilling to promptly elevate retrieval performance.
We show that previous backfilling strategies suffer from decreased performance and demonstrate the importance of both the training objective and the ordering in <em id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">online</em> partial backfilling.
We propose a new training method for feature alignment between old and new embedding models using uncertainty estimation. Compared to previous works, we obtain significantly improved backfilling results on a variety of datasets: mAP on ImageNet (+4.4%), Places-365 (+2.7%), and VGG-Face2 (+1.3%). Further, we demonstrate that when updating a biased model with FastFill, the minority subgroup accuracy gap promptly vanishes with a small fraction of partial backfilling.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
        Code available at <a href="https://github.com/apple/ml-fct" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/apple/ml-fct</a>.</span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Retrieval problems have become increasingly popular for many real-life applications such as face recognition, voice recognition, image localization, and object identification. In an image retrieval setup, we have a large set of images called the gallery set with predicted labels and a set of unknown query images. The aim of image retrieval is to match query images to related images in the gallery set, ideally of the same class/identity.
In practice, we use low-dimensional feature vectors generated by a learned embedding model instead of the original high dimensional images to perform retrieval.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2303.04766v1/compatibility_figure_new.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:302/179;" width="302" height="179" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2303.04766v1/fig1b-alt2.svg" id="S1.F1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:192/187;" width="192" height="187"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Left:</span>
Old and new features for a binary fruits vs. animals classification setup. Old and new features are somewhat compatible, but have a few mismatches shown by red crosses (top). We can improve retrieval performance by backfilling some of the old features to higher quality new features in a specific order (bottom). In a partial backfilling scenario the accuracy improvement depends on the order of backfilling. <span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Right:</span> Retrieval performance for ImageNet as a function of time when updating the embedding model with different backfilling strategies. A backfilling curve reaching the new model performance faster is better.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When we get access to more or better training data, model architectures, or training regimes we want to update the embedding model to improve the performance of the downstream retrieval task. However, different neural networks rarely learn to generate compatible features even when they have been trained on the same dataset, with the same optimization method, and have the same architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2015</a>)</cite>. Hence, computing the query features with a new embedding model, whilst keeping the old gallery features, leads to poor retrieval results due to incompatibility of old and new embedding models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The vanilla solution is to replace the features in the gallery set that have been generated by the old model with features from the new model. This computationally expensive process is called <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">backfilling</em>.
In practice, we carry out backfilling <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">offline</em>: we carry on using the old gallery features and the old model for queries whilst computing new gallery features with the new model in the background (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-right). We only use the new gallery features once we’ve finished updating the entire set. However, for large scale systems this process is computationally expensive and can take months. In many real world systems, the cost of backfilling is a blocker for model updates, despite the availability of a more accurate model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">This has led rise to the study of compatible representation learning. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al. (2020)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Budnik &amp; Avrithis (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duggal et al. (2021)</a></cite> all proposed methods to update the embedding model to achieve better performance whilst still being compatible with features generated by the old model (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-left-top).
Despite relative success, compatibility learning is not perfect: performing retrieval with a mixture of old and new features achieves lower accuracies than when we replace all the old features with new ones.
In this work, we focus on closing this performance gap. Further, some previous methods degrade the new model performance when trying to make it more compatible with the old model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hu et al., 2022</a>)</cite> or requiring availability of side-information, extra features from a separate self-supervised model, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al., 2022</a>)</cite> (which may not be available for an existing system). We relax both constraints in this work.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To benefit from the more accurate embedding model sooner and cheaper, we can backfill some or all of the images in an <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">online</em> continuous fashion: We run downstream retrieval tasks on a partially backfilled gallery set where part of the features are computed with the old model, and part of them with the new model (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-left-bottom).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we can consider two scenarios: 1) we will backfill the entire gallery set with a <em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">random order</em> in an extended period of time and want to maximize the average performance during the backfilling process (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-right); 2) we have a fixed partial backfilling budget and want to reach optimal retrieval performance after backfilling the allowed number of images (e.g., we can backfill only <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the gallery). In both cases, we want to reach the highest possible performance by backfilling the fewest images possible.
We demonstrate that the training objective as well as the order by which we backfill images are both crucial. In fact, if we use training losses proposed in the literature and choose a random ordering we may even reduce performance before we see an improvement (see FCT-Random in Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf1" title="Figure 2(a) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a>) due to the occurrence of ‘negative flips’ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>)</cite> - images that where classified correctly when using the old model but are misclassified when using the new one.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we propose FastFill: an efficient compatible representation learning and online backfilling method resulting in prompt retrieval accuracy boosts as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-right. In FastFill, we learn a computationally efficient holistic transformation to align feature vectors from the old model embedding space to that of new model. The new model is trained independently without sacrificing its performance for compatibility. We propose a new training loss that contains point-to-point and point-to-cluster objectives. We train the transformation model with the proposed loss using uncertainty estimation and obtain significantly improved partial backfilling performance compared to previous works.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We summarize our main contribution as below:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose FastFill, a new compatible training method with improved retrieval performance at all levels of partial backfilling compared to previous works.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">FastFill uses a novel training objective and a new policy to order samples to be backfilled which we show to be critical for improved performance.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate the application of FastFill to update biased embedding models with minimum compute, crucial to efficiently fix large-scale biased retrieval systems.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On a variety of datasets we demonstrate FastFill obtains state-of-the-art results: mAP on ImageNet (+4.4%), Places-365 (+2.7%), and VGG-Face2 (+1.3%).</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Problem setup</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Image Retrieval</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In an image retrieval system, we have a set of images called the gallery set <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> with predicted labels, which can be separated into <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> different classes or clusters. At inference time, we further have a query set <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>. For each image in the query set we aim to retrieve an image from the gallery set of the same class.
In an embedding based retrieval system, we replace the original <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional data (<math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3\times h\times w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3\times h\times w</annotation></semantics></math> for images) in the gallery and query sets with features generated by a trained embedding model <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi:\mathbb{R}^{D}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>D</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi:\mathbb{R}^{D}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\ll D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\ll D</annotation></semantics></math>. The model <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϕ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi</annotation></semantics></math> is trained on images <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, a disjoint dataset from both <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For a query image <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{q}\in\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{q}\in\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math>, the retrieval algorithm returns image <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> from the gallery satisfying:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{(single-model retrieval)}\hskip 14.22636pt{\bm{x}}_{i}=\argmin_{{\bm{x}}_{j}\in\mathcal{G}}\mathfrak{D}(\phi({\bm{x}}_{j}),\phi({\bm{x}}_{q}))," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>(single-model retrieval)</mtext><mspace style="width:1.42em;" width="1.42em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mi>𝔇</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{(single-model retrieval)}\hskip 14.22636pt{\bm{x}}_{i}=\argmin_{{\bm{x}}_{j}\in\mathcal{G}}\mathfrak{D}(\phi({\bm{x}}_{j}),\phi({\bm{x}}_{q})),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">for some distance function <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathfrak{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝔇</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathfrak{D}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> or cosine distance). In this setup we only need to compute the features <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi({\bm{x}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi({\bm{x}})</annotation></semantics></math> of the gallery set once and store them for future queries. We then no longer need to be able to access the original images of the gallery. As <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d\ll D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\ll D</annotation></semantics></math>, replacing the images with their features greatly reduces the memory and computational requirement to maintain the gallery and perform retrieval, crucial for private on-device retrieval. Depending on the context, by gallery we may refer to the original images or the corresponding features.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Learning Compatible Representations.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For real world applications, we aim to update the embedding model every few months to improve its accuracy 1) to adapt to changes in the world, e.g., supporting people with face mask for a face recognition system, 2) on under-represented subgroups, e.g., new ethnicity, new lighting condition, different data capture sensors, by adding more data to the training set, or 3) by using enhanced architecture and training optimization. We denote the old and new embedding models by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{old}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}</annotation></semantics></math> and the training datasets of the two models by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{old}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{new}</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
After a model update, for every new query image we use <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}</annotation></semantics></math> to compute the feature, and hence the retrieval task turns in to:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{(cross-model retrieval)}\hskip 14.22636pt{\bm{x}}_{i}=\argmin_{{\bm{x}}_{j}\in\mathcal{G}}\mathfrak{D}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{j}),\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{q}))." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>(cross-model retrieval)</mtext><mspace style="width:1.42em;" width="1.42em"></mspace><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>min</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mi>𝔇</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>old</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mi>new</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{(cross-model retrieval)}\hskip 14.22636pt{\bm{x}}_{i}=\argmin_{{\bm{x}}_{j}\in\mathcal{G}}\mathfrak{D}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{j}),\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{q})).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2015)</a></cite> realised, different models do not always generate compatible features, even when they are trained on the same dataset.
This observation has motivated the rise of the relatively new literature on model compatibility: given a weaker old model <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{old}</annotation></semantics></math> we aim to train a new model <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}</annotation></semantics></math> that has better retrieval performance, as in (<a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ Image Retrieval ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), whilst still is compatible with the old model, as in (<a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Learning Compatible Representations. ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). This way we can improve performance, without having to wait months and incur large computational cost to backfill the gallery.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al. (2020)</a></cite> introduced Backwards Compatible Training (BCT). They add an influence loss term to the new model objective that runs the old model linear classifier on the features generated by the new model to encourage compatibility.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Budnik &amp; Avrithis (2021)</a></cite> train a new model by formulating backward-compatible regularization as a contrastive loss.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2021)</a></cite> proposed a Regression-Alleviating Compatible Training (RACT) method that adds a regularization term to the contrastive loss in order to reduce <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">negative flips</em>: these are images that the old model classified correctly but the new model gets wrong.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al. (2022)</a></cite> proposed the Forward Compatible Training (FCT) method that trains an independent new model first and subsequently trains a transformation function which maps features from old model embedding space to that of the new model. Moreover, the transformation requires some side-information about each data point as input. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Iscen et al. (2020)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2020)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al. (2022)</a></cite> also approach the model compatibility problem by learning maps between old and new model embedding spaces. Note that, as discussed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al. (2022)</a></cite> the cost of applying the transformation is negligible compared to running the embedding model on images (hence, the instant jump in performance in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-right).</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Learning Compatible Predictions.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A related line of research focuses on learning compatible predictions (as opposed to compatible features).
For the classification task, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Srivastava et al. (2020)</a></cite> show that changing the random seed can lead to high prediction incompatibility even when the rest of the learning setup stays constant. Moreover, they observed incompatible points do not always have low confidence scores.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oesterling &amp; Sapiro (2021)</a></cite> aim to achieve better prediction compatible models by ensuring that the new model training loss is smaller than the old model loss on all training samples.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Träuble et al. (2021)</a></cite> consider the problem of assigning labels to a large unlabelled dataset. In particular, they focus on how to determine which points to re-classify when given a new model and how to proceed if the old and new predictions differ from each other.
Similar to compatible representation learning, various works in the literature focus on positive-congruent training which aims to reduce the number of negative flips in the prediction setting. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yan et al. (2021)</a></cite> achieve this by focal distillation which puts a greater emphasis on samples that the old model classifies correctly. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2022)</a></cite> argue that most negative flips are caused by logits with large margins and thus try to reduce large logit displacement.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Continual Learning (CL) and Knowledge Distillation (KD).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Other less relevant areas of research that focus on learning across domains and tasks include CL and KD.
CL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Parisi et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li &amp; Hoiem, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zenke et al., 2017</a>)</cite> is related to compatible learning as it also aims to train a new model that should keep the knowledge acquired by the old one. However, in the continual learning setup the new model is dealing with a new task, whereas here the task (image retrieval) is fixed. Also, in CL the two models never interact as they are not employed together: as soon as the new model is trained we discard the old one.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In KD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hinton et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gou et al., 2021</a>)</cite> we also train a new model (the student) that inherits some of the capabilities of an old model (the teacher). However, there are two main differences to model compatibility setup. Firstly, in KD the teacher model is often a larger and stronger model than the student, reverse of the setup in model compatibility. Further, the teacher and the student are never used together in practice. Therefore, the features of the two models do not need to be compatible in the KD setting. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2021)</a></cite> show that neither CL methods nor KD ones are able to achieve good retrieval performance in the model update setting as the features of the old and new models are not compatible.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Feature alignment</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some previous works aim to achieve model compatibility when training the new model, by directly enforcing new features to be aligned to the existing old model features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Budnik &amp; Avrithis, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
However, this often greatly reduces the single model retrieval performance defined in Eq. (<a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ Image Retrieval ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) for the new model, as they suffer from the inherent trade-off between maximizing the new model performance and at the same time its compatibility to the weaker old model.
Other works have thus proposed learning a separate mapping from old model embedding space to new model embedding space to align their features <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2020)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meng et al. (2021)</a></cite> both still modify the training of the new model which is undesirable because it can limit the performance gain of the new model and is intrusive and complicated for practitioners. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al. (2022)</a></cite> train the new model and alignment map independently, but to achieve better alignment rely on existence of side-information (an extra feature generated by an unsupervised model computed for each data point). This is also undesirable because is not applicable to an already existing system without side-information available. We provide results in the presence of such side-information in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Side-Information Experiments ‣ Appendix B Further Experimental Results ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.
Here, as a baseline we consider the same feature alignment as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al. (2022)</a></cite>, but without side-information: we learn a map <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> from old model feature space to new model feature space modeled by an MLP architecture with parameters <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>. Hence, for cross-model retrieval we use <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{j}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{j}))</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. (<a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Learning Compatible Representations. ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>FastFill</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite relative success, all previous methods have limitations and fail to reach full-compatibility:
in each case cross-model retrieval defined in Eq. (<a href="#S2.E2" title="Equation 2 ‣ Learning Compatible Representations. ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) has significantly worse performance than single-model retrieval defined in Eq. (<a href="#S2.E1" title="Equation 1 ‣ Image Retrieval ‣ 2 Problem setup ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) with the new model.
In order to bridge this gap, (partial) backfilling is required: continuously move from cross model retrieval to single model retrieval by updating the old gallery features with the new model.
That is to replace transformed old features <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math> with new features <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> for some or all images in the gallery set <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathcal{G})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathcal{G})</annotation></semantics></math> (Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>);
To this end, we propose our new method FastFill, which includes two main contributions: firstly, we change the
backfilling curve behaviour for a random policy by modifying the alignment model training and secondly, we introduce a better policy that produces the order of samples to update, therefore results in promptly closing the gap between cross-model and single-model retrieval.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a training loss for the alignment map <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> to have both high retrieval performance at no backfilling (the instant jump after model update in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>-right) and good backfilling curve, ensuring that we close the gap with new model performance promptly. To achieve this, we include objectives to encourage point-to-point and point-to-cluster alignments.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The first part of our training loss is the pairwise squared distance between the new features and the transformed old features: <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}({\bm{x}};h_{\theta},\phi_{old},\phi_{new})=\|\phi_{new}({\bm{x}})-h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}))\|^{2}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}({\bm{x}};h_{\theta},\phi_{old},\phi_{new})=\|\phi_{new}({\bm{x}})-h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}))\|^{2}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{D}_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}\in\mathcal{D}_{new}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is the loss used by FCT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ramanujan et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Further, given <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{old}</annotation></semantics></math> and the new model classifier head, <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{new}</annotation></semantics></math>, that the new model has been trained on, we use a discriminative loss that runs <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{new}</annotation></semantics></math> on the transformed features: <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{disc}({\bm{x}},y;h_{\theta},\phi_{old},\kappa_{new})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{disc}({\bm{x}},y;h_{\theta},\phi_{old},\kappa_{new})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="({\bm{x}},y)\in\mathcal{D}_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">({\bm{x}},y)\in\mathcal{D}_{new}</annotation></semantics></math> is a pair of (image, label).
<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{disc}</annotation></semantics></math> is the same discriminative loss that new model is trained on: in our experiments it is the Cross Entropy loss with Label Smoothing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Szegedy et al., 2016</a>)</cite> for ImageNet-1k and Places-365 datasets, and the ArcFace loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2019</a>)</cite> for VGGFace2 dataset.
This loss can be thought of as the reverse of the influence loss in BCT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2020</a>)</cite> but with one major advantage. Unlike BCT, we do not require old and new models to have been trained on the same classes as we are using the new model classifier head rather than the old one.
Our proposed alignment loss is a combination of the two losses:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}(h_{\theta};\phi_{old},\phi_{new},\kappa_{new},{\bm{x}},y)=\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}+\mathcal{L}_{disc}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}(h_{\theta};\phi_{old},\phi_{new},\kappa_{new},{\bm{x}},y)=\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}+\mathcal{L}_{disc}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> achieves pairwise compatibility, aligning each transformed old feature with the corresponding new feature. However, in practice we cannot obtain a perfect alignment on unseen data in the query and gallery sets. With <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> we encourage to reduce the magnitude of pair-wise alignment error <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})-h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})-h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math>, but the direction of error is free. <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{disc}</annotation></semantics></math> encourages the error vectors to be oriented towards the same-class clusters of the new model (given by <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>κ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa_{new}</annotation></semantics></math>) and away from wrong clusters. Hence, we avoid proximity of a cluster of transformed old features to a wrong cluster of new features – the mechanism responsible of slow improvements in backfilling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We now focus on coming up with good ordering to backfill the images in the gallery set (replacing <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math>’s with <math id="S4.SS2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>’s). Finding <em id="S4.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">the optimal</em> ordering for backfilling is a hard combinatorial problem and infeasible. We first look at a heuristically good (but cheating) ordering: backfill the worst gallery features first. As minimizing the alignment loss (<a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) leads to good transformation function, we use it as a way to measure the quality of the gallery features: we compute the training loss (<a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) for each image in the gallery set and sort the images in decreasing order. In other words, we backfill the gallery images with the highest loss first as they are probably not very compatible with the new model. We call this method FastFill-Cheating.
We show in Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf1" title="Figure 2(a) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a> that using FastFill-Cheating results in significantly better backfilling curve than when we backfill using a random ordering.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Unfortunately, we cannot use this backfilling method in practice for images in the gallery as we do not have access to <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> until we have backfilled the <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>th image. Instead, we aim to estimate this ordering borrowing ideas from Bayesian Deep Learning.
When the training objective is <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we can model the alignment error by a multivariate Gaussian distribution with <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma\mathbb{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝕀</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma\mathbb{I}</annotation></semantics></math> covariance matrix<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            We also considered an arbitrary diagonal covariance matrix instead of a scaled identity matrix, and observed no significant improvement.</span></span></span>, and reduce the negative log likelihood during training. This is similar to the method proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kendall &amp; Gal (2017)</a></cite>. Given the old and new models, we train a model <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{\vartheta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\mapsto\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>ϑ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{\vartheta}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\mapsto\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> parameterized by <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϑ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta</annotation></semantics></math> that takes the old model feature <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\phi_{old})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\phi_{old})</annotation></semantics></math> as input and estimate <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. We can then jointly train <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{\vartheta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>ϑ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{\vartheta}</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{new}}\left[\frac{\|h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}))-\phi_{new}({\bm{x}})\|^{2}_{2}}{\sigma^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\log\sigma^{2}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>𝒙</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>λ</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{x}}\sim\mathcal{D}_{new}}\left[\frac{\|h_{\theta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}))-\phi_{new}({\bm{x}})\|^{2}_{2}}{\sigma^{2}}+\dfrac{1}{\lambda}\log\sigma^{2}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\sigma^{2}=\psi_{\vartheta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>ϑ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒙</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\sigma^{2}=\psi_{\vartheta}(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}))</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is a hyper-parameter function of <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. Now, we extend this formulation for our multi-objective training in (<a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>). We follow the approximation in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kendall et al. (2018)</a></cite> for uncertainty estimation in a multi-task setup where the model has both a discrete and continuous output. Further, we assume the same covariance parameter, <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, for both of our regression and discriminative objectives (<math id="S4.SS2.p7.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l2}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{disc}</annotation></semantics></math>).
Hence, we can replace <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> in (<a href="#S4.E4" title="Equation 4 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) with <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}</annotation></semantics></math> and get the full FastFill training loss:</p>
<table id="S4.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
