</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p7.3" class="ltx_p">In practice, we use a shared backbone for <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{\vartheta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>ϑ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{\vartheta}</annotation></semantics></math>, therefore the overhead is minimal. Please see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Training Set-Up ‣ Appendix A Experimental Set-Up ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a> for details of architecture, hyper-parameters, and training setup.
In Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf2" title="Figure 2(b) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(b)</span></a> we show that the predicted <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{\vartheta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>ϑ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{\vartheta}</annotation></semantics></math> trained with (<a href="#S4.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) is a good approximation of <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>. In particular, the ordering implied by <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> are close. In Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf3" title="Figure 2(c) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(c)</span></a> we show the order of each <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the gallery when sorted by <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m28" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> is well correlated with its order when sorted by <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m29" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>: The Kendall-Tau correlation between two orderings is 0.67 on the ImageNet test set. In FastFill, we backfill <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m30" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>’s with the ordering implied by their predicted <math id="S4.SS2.p7.m31" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>’s (from high to low values).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, in Figure <a href="#S4.F2.sf1" title="Figure 2(a) ‣ Figure 2 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2(a)</span></a> we show that FastFill obtains similar backfilling curve as the cheating setup using the ordering implied by cheaply computed <math id="S4.SS2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>’s. Also note that, FastFill even with a random ordering obtains significant improvement compared to our baseline (FCT with random ordering) due to superiority of our proposed alignment loss. In Section <a href="#S6" title="6 Ablation study ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> we further demonstrate the importance of our proposed training objective and backfilling ordering.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F2.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/imagenet_cheating-map.png" id="S4.F2.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/312;" width="548" height="312" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F2.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/correlation_sigma_vs_log_loss_no_rank.png" id="S4.F2.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/525;" width="548" height="525" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F2.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/correlation_sigma_vs_disc_plus_pairwise.png" id="S4.F2.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:548/485;" width="548" height="485" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(c) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
a) Backfilling results for different training objectives and backfilling orderings evaluated on the ImageNet-1k dataset. The FastFill training objective, defined in Eqn. (<a href="#S4.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>), compared to our baseline method (FCT) obtains significantly improved mAP over the course of backfilling when a random ordering is used. The performance is further improved when using the ordering implied by the predicted uncertainties <math id="S4.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. We also compare against FastFill-Cheating, in which the ordering is obtained by computing the training loss (<a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) on gallery images (hence a cheating setup), and show comparable performance.
b) We show that the predicted <math id="S4.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, the output of <math id="S4.F2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{\vartheta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>ϑ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{\vartheta}</annotation></semantics></math> on gallery images, and <math id="S4.F2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> are well correlated.
c) We sort <math id="S4.F2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> once by <math id="S4.F2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma_{i}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>σ</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma_{i}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and once by <math id="S4.F2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> to get two orderings. Here, for each <math id="S4.F2.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> we plot its order in the first ordering vs its order in the second ordering, and observe great correlation (Kendall-Tau correlation=0.67).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now analyse the performance of our method by comparing it against different baselines on a variety of datasets. We first describe the metrics we use to evaluate and compare different compatibility and backfilling methods.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h3>

<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compatibility Metrics</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to previous model compatibility works we mainly use following two metrics to evaluate the performance and compatibility of models.
The <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cumulative Matching Characteristics (CMC)</span> evaluates the top-<math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> retrieval accuracy. We compute the distance between a single query feature and every single gallery features. We then return the <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> gallery features with the smallest distance. If at least one of the <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> returned gallery images has the same label as the query we consider the retrieval to be successful. We also compute the <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">mean Average Precision (mAP)</span> score, which calculates the area under the precision-recall curve over recall values between 0.0 and 1.0.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given a metric <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> (either top-<math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> CMC or mAP), a gallery set <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, and query set <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Q}</annotation></semantics></math> we denote the retrieval performance by <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{Q})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{Q})</annotation></semantics></math>. After a model update, we use <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}</annotation></semantics></math> to compute features for the query set and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{old}</annotation></semantics></math> to compute those for the gallery set. Similar to previous works, for retrieval metrics, we use the full validation/test set of each dataset as both the query set and gallery set. When we perform a query with an image, we remove it from the gallery set to avoid a trivial match.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Backfilling Metrics</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In partial backfilling we replace some of the old features, here <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\phi_{old}({\bm{x}}_{i}))</annotation></semantics></math>), from the gallery with new features, <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}({\bm{x}}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>.
In order to evaluate the retrieval performance for a partially backfilled gallery we introduce the following notation:
given an ordering <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi:{\bm{x}}_{\pi_{1}},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\pi_{n}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi:{\bm{x}}_{\pi_{1}},\ldots,{\bm{x}}_{\pi_{n}}</annotation></semantics></math> of the images in the gallery set and a backfilling fraction <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math>, we define <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{\pi,\alpha}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{\pi,\alpha}</annotation></semantics></math> to be the partially backfilled gallery set. We use the new model to compute features for <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\pi[:n_{\alpha}]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\pi[:n_{\alpha}]</annotation></semantics></math> and the old model for the remaining images, that is for all <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\pi[n_{\alpha}:]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>π</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\pi[n_{\alpha}:]</annotation></semantics></math>, using numpy array notation, where <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\alpha}=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>α</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌊</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⌋</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\alpha}=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the size of gallery.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Given a metric <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, to compare different backfilling and model update strategies during the entire course of model update, we propose the following averaged quantity:</p>
<table id="S5.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{M}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{Q},\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\alpha\sim[0,1]}M(\mathcal{G}_{\pi,\alpha},\mathcal{Q})" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>M</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒬</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{M}(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{Q},\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\alpha\sim[0,1]}M(\mathcal{G}_{\pi,\alpha},\mathcal{Q})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> can be any retrieval metric such as top-<math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> CMC or mAP as defined above. The backfilling metric <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mi>M</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{M}</annotation></semantics></math> corresponds to the area under the backfilling curve for evaluation with <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Backfilling Experiments</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now analyse our method by comparing it to three baselines: BCT, RACT, and FCT. For BCT and FCT we used the official implementation provided by the authors. We re-implemented RACT and optimized over the hyper-parameters as the code was not publicly available at the time of writing. We ran all experiments five times with different random seeds and report the averaged results.
We use the <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> distance for image retrieval.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.SS2.tab1" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<div id="S5.SS2.tab1.1" class="ltx_block ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:258.4pt;"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/imagenet_two_in_one.png" id="S5.SS2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:357/176;" width="357" height="176" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
</div></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.SS2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle" style="width:131.2pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 1: </span>ImageNet-1k </figcaption>
<table id="S5.SS2.fig1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S5.SS2.fig1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ImageNet-1k.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare FastFill against BCT, RACT, and FCT, three state-of-the-art methods. For RACT we use entropy-backfilling; since BCT and FCT do not offer a policy for backfilling we use random orders. FastFill outperforms all three methods by over 3.5% for <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{CMC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>CMC</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{CMC}}</annotation></semantics></math>-top1 and over 4% for <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{mAP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>mAP</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{mAP}}</annotation></semantics></math> (Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Backfilling Experiments ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, Table <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Backfilling Experiments ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>).
Compared to BCT and RACT, FastFill performs significantly better for 0% backfilling (+10%) due to the transformation function. Furthermore, the sigma-based ordering significantly outperforms the random orderings and the cross-entropy one from RACT. We show in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Positive and Negative Flips Analysis ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> that FastFill both increases the number of positive flips and decreases the negative flips compared to FCT.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">VGGFace2.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show results on the VGGFace2 dataset in Table <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Backfilling Experiments ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Backfilling Experiments ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
FastFill improves the baselines as well as an ablation that combines entropy-based backfilling with the FastFill transformation by 0.5% <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{CMC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>CMC</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{CMC}}</annotation></semantics></math>-top1 and 1.3% <math id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{mAP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>mAP</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{mAP}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The absolute improvement is relatively small as the gap between 0% and 100% backfilling is not very large, as the transformation already achieves high compatibility.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Places-365.</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run experiments on the Places-365 dataset. The results are summarized in Table <a href="#S5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Backfilling Experiments ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S5.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Backfilling Experiments ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. FastFill beats FCT with random backfilling by about 2.7% for both metrics.
We further report CMC-top5 results in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 CMC-top5 ‣ Appendix B Further Experimental Results ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a> for all three datasets.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Updating biased models</h3>

<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:38%;"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/fairness.png" id="S5.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:192/191;" width="192" height="191" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Embedding models can be biased toward certain sub-groups in their input domain, a crucial problem in image retrieval. For example, in face recognition tasks the model can be biased toward a certain ethnicity, gender, or face attribute. It is often due to a class-imbalanced training dataset. Here, we show FastFill can fix model biases efficiently without requiring expensive full backfilling. We train a biased old model on the VGGFace2-Gender-550 dataset that consists of 50 female and 500 males classes. The old model performs significantly better on males identities (90.6%) in the test set than females (68.7%).
We train a new model on a larger gender-balanced dataset that consists of 2183 female and 2183 male identities. The new model still has a small bias towards male classes (98.3% vs 97.1%).
Applying the feature alignment trained with FastFill alleviates some of the biases reducing the accuracy gap between genders to 9.4%.
As we show in Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.3 Updating biased models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, with only 25% backfilling FastFill reaches the same accuracy gap between genders as the new model, whereas random backfilling using FCT requires backfilling the entire gallery set to reduce the bias to the level of the new model.
FastFill prioritizes backfilling instances corresponding to female identities which results in a fast reduction in the gender gap compared to previous methods (see Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Backfilling Order Analysis - VGGFace2-Gender ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Ablation study</h2>

<figure id="S6.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/ablation_with_numbers_legend_top.png" id="S6.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:220/265;" width="220" height="265" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Ablation Study on ImageNet: We compare the effect of different training losses and backfilling orderings on the backfilling curves. We report <math id="S6.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{mAP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>mAP</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{mAP}}</annotation></semantics></math> in the parentheses in the legend.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Here, we perform an ablation study to highlight the different components of our method (Figure <a href="#S6.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 6 Ablation study ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
We first compare the effect of different training losses (<math id="S6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{disc}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}</annotation></semantics></math> with and without uncertainty) when using random backfilling orderings.
We show that <math id="S6.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}</annotation></semantics></math> greatly improves the backfilling curve. Training with uncertainty has little effect on random backfilling.
We also show that using <math id="S6.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> for the backfilling ordering greatly improves performance.
We conclude that FastFill (training with <math id="S6.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}</annotation></semantics></math> and uncertainty) obtains the best results for both random and <math id="S6.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>-based orderings.
We show in Appendices <a href="#A3.SS3" title="C.3 Ablation on ImageNet-250 to ImageNet-500 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_italic"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.3</span></a> and <a href="#A3.SS4" title="C.4 Ablation on VGGFace2 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_italic"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C.4</span></a> that FastFill is particularly strong when we encounter new classes at inference time as the relative confidence (used in RACT) between samples from new classes are not as informative.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Model compatibility is a crucial problem in many large-scale retrieval systems and a common blocker to update embedding models. In this work, we propose FastFill: an online model update strategy to efficiently close the accuracy gap of previous model compatibility works.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The key idea in FastFill is to perform partial backfilling: using a new model we recompute a small fraction of the images from a large gallery set. To make the partial backfilling process efficient we propose a new training objective for the alignment model which maps the old model features to those of the new model, and an ordering of the gallery images to perform backfilling. To obtain the ordering we train the alignment model using uncertainty estimation and use predicted uncertainties to order the images in the gallery set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We demonstrate superior performance compared to previous works on several datasets. More importantly, we show that using FastFill a biased old model can be efficiently fixed without requiring full backfilling.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="S8" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">8 </span>ETHICS STATEMENT</h2>

<div id="S8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We believe that FastFill can have a positive impact in real-world applications by reducing the cost associated with model update, and hence enable frequent model updates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Machine learning based models are often not completely unbiased and require regular updates when we become aware of a certain limitation and/or bias. As shown in the paper, when we have a new model with fewer biases than an existing model, FastFill can reach the fairness level of the new model more quickly and cheaply. This can motivate frequent model updates to address limitations associated with under represented groups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S8.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As with many machine learning applications, especially ones used for facial recognition, FastFill can be misused. Facial recognition software can be used in many unethical settings, so improving their performance can have significant downsides as well as upsides.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S9" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">9 </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="S9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our proposed method does not provide a mechanism to decide what percentage of backfilling is sufficient to enable early stopping. Knowing how much backfilling is sufficient would result in saving additional computation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S9.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S9.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In some real world applications, the image representations can be used in a more sophisticated fashion by the downstream task than the nearest neighbour based retrieval considered in this work. For instance, representations can be input to another trained model. Therefore, when we update from old to new, we also need to retrain the downstream model so it is compatible with new feature space. This is not a limitation of FastFill in particular, however, in general a limitation of transformation based update methods.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Experimental Set-Up</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Dataset Set-Up</h3>

<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ImageNet-1k <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">ImageNet-1k is a large-scale image recognition dataset and the most used subset of ImageNet [ILSVRC]. It was used in the ILSVRC 2012 image recognition challenge. The dataset contains 1000 object classes and a total of 1,281,167 training images and 50,000 validation images. The training dataset is relatively balanced with about 1.2k images per class. The validation set has the same classes as the training set and exactly 500 images per class.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use a subset of ImageNet-1k consisting of the first 500 classes to train the old model; we refer to this as ImageNet-500. We note that the first half of ImageNet-1k contains easier classes than the second half.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Places-365 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Places-365 is a large-scale scene recognition dataset that spans 365 classes and contains 1.8 million training images and 36,500 validation ones. The training set contains between 3068 and 5000 images per category and the validation set has exactly 100 images per class. We use the first 182 classes of the training set to create a smaller subset; we refer to it as Places-182.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">VGGFace2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>)</cite>.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">VGGFace2 is a large-scale facial recognition dataset. Its training dataset is made up of 8631 classes, each representing a different person, and a total of 3.14 million images. The test set contains 170,000 images corresponding to 500 identities, different to the ones present in the training set. The training set is slightly unbalanced with an average of 362.6, a minimum of 57, and a maximum of 843 images per class. The test set contains exactly 500 images per class. During test time, we compute a random but fixed subsample of 50 images per class in the test set.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The dataset also has a list of attributes for a small number of images in the training dataset. We know the gender of 30,000 images corresponding to 5300 different identities. We create a training and validation set of images for which we know the gender as follows: we disregard all the images in the training set with an unknown gender. We randomly sample 250 female identities and 250 male ones to form the new validation set.
As there are more male than female classes remaining, we sample a subset of the remaining male identities to create a balanced training dataset (2183 female and male classes each with about 800,000 images for either (exact numbers depend on the random seed)). We refer to this new subset as <span id="A1.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VGGFace2-Gender</span>. We now create an unbalanced subset by sampling 500 male identities and 50 female identities from the training set, we name it VGGFace2-Gender-550. We use this dataset to train a biased old model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Training Set-Up</h3>

<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ImageNet-1k.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train two ResNet50 models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>)</cite>: the old model (<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{old}</annotation></semantics></math>) on ImageNet-500, and the new model (<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi_{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ϕ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi_{new}</annotation></semantics></math>), on ImageNet-1k. We set the embedding dimension of both models to 128.
We train both models using the hyper-parameters in ResNetV1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nvidia (17)</a></cite> (SGD optimizer, epochs=100, batchsize=1024, learning rate=1.024, weight decay=<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="3.0517578125*10^{-5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>3.0517578125</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">3.0517578125*10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math>, momentum=0.875, cosine learning rate decay with 5 epochs of linear warmup).
For our method, we jointly train a transformation model <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, and an uncertainty predictor <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math> on ImageNet-1k using the objective function defined above (<a href="#S4.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 FastFill ‣ 4 Method ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>).
We use the same architecture for the MLP architecture for the transformation function <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>)</cite> and the same learning set-up (Adam <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma &amp; Ba (13)</a></cite>, epochs=80, learning rate=<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5*10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∗</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5*10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, cosine learning rate decay with 5 epochs of linear warm-up, freeze of the BatchNorm layers after 40 epochs).
For the uncertainty estimator <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>, we simply use a linear layer from the transformed embeddings space to output a single real value.
For FCT, we train their transformation without side-information exactly as described in their paper and their official code base (<a href="https://github.com/apple/ml-fct" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/apple/ml-fct</a>).
For BCT we train a new model using the official code implementation (<a href="https://github.com/YantaoShen/openBCT" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/YantaoShen/openBCT</a>) and hyper-parameters mentioned in the paper. However, we set the embedding dimension to 128 to be directly comparable to the other three models.
For RACT, we re-implement the method based on the information provided in the paper as there is no official code release. We set the hyper-parameters (<math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=1</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>) as defined in the paper and optimize over the learning rate to get optimal performance.
We compare the learning rate schedule used in RACT with the one used in ResNet50V1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nvidia (17)</a></cite>. optimizing over the learning rate for each (we try learning rates in powers of ten in [1e-5, 1]).</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the retrieval experiments we set both the gallery and query sets to be the validation set of ImageNet-1k.
For BCT and FCT we use random backfilling, as neither paper include a backfilling ordering. For RACT we try both random backfilling and entropy backfilling and pick the better one.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Places-365.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a similar setup to ImageNet experiments: we train two ResNet50 models with an embedding size of 512: the old model on Places-182 and the new one on Places-365. We use the Places-365 validation dataset for retrieval evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">VGGFace2.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For the VGGFace2 dataset we train a smaller ResNet18 model on VGGFace2-863 and a larger ResNet50 one on VGGFace2-8631. Unlike for the other two datasets we use the ArcFace objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>)</cite> to train the two models and the transformation. We use a margin of 0.5 and a scale of 64 as proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>)</cite>. We use the same learning rate schedule as for ImageNet. Unlike for the other two datasets we normalize the features.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Further Experimental Results</h2>

<section id="A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Architectural Change Experiments</h3>

<div id="A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyse how FastFill compares to existing methods when the old and new models have different architectures. We run ImageNet experiments where the old model is a ResNet-18, and the new model a ResNet-50. Both are trained on the same full ImageNet-1k training set. As before, we repeat the experiments with 5 random seeds and illustrate the results in Table <a href="#A2.T4.fig1" title="Table 4 ‣ B.1 Architectural Change Experiments ‣ Appendix B Further Experimental Results ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and Figure <a href="#A2.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ B.1 Architectural Change Experiments ‣ Appendix B Further Experimental Results ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.
The overall trends are the same as the other setups in the original paper. FastFill significantly outperforms all baselines.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Side-Information Experiments</h3>

<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span>We add side-information to the transformation function trained with either FastFill (blue) or FCT (orange). FastFill outperforms FCT on all three metrics: CMC-top1 (left), CMC-top5 (middle), and mAP (right).</figcaption><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/imagenet_side_info.png" id="A2.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/158;" width="548" height="158" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure>
<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now train both the FCT transformation model (<math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>) as well as the FastFill transformation and uncertainty models (<math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ψ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi</annotation></semantics></math>) with side-information. For the side-information model we train a ResNet50 model on ImageNet-500 with SimCLR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>)</cite>. Otherwise, we use the same set-up as for the main paper ImageNet experiments. We show in Figure <a href="#A2.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ B.2 Side-Information Experiments ‣ Appendix B Further Experimental Results ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> that both methods get a performance boost with side-information. But FastFill still significantly outperforms FCT on three different metrics: <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{CMC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>CMC</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{CMC}}</annotation></semantics></math>-top1 (67.81% vs 64.72%), <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{CMC}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>CMC</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{CMC}}</annotation></semantics></math>-top5 (84.23% vs 82.35%), and <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\widetilde{\text{mAP}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mover accent="true"><mtext>mAP</mtext><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\widetilde{\text{mAP}}</annotation></semantics></math> (46.23% vs 42.55%).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>CMC-top5</h3>

<div id="A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run experiments using the CMC-top5 retrieval metric. As shown Figure <a href="#A2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ B.3 CMC-top5 ‣ Appendix B Further Experimental Results ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> FastFill outperforms all baselines on ImageNet-1k (+2.8%), VGGFace2 (0.1%), and Places-365 (+2.1%) when using CMC-top5 to evaluate retrieval performance.</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Further Ablation Studies</h2>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Ablation on ImageNet-1k</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We elaborate from the ablation study provided in the main paper in section <a href="#S6" title="6 Ablation study ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> in Figure <a href="#A3.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ Table 5 ‣ C.1 Ablation on ImageNet-1k ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> and Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ C.1 Ablation on ImageNet-1k ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> adding the CMC-top1 metric. In particular we show that when training with <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{disc}</annotation></semantics></math> with or without uncertainty we get poor compatibility performance at 0% backfilling and throughout the backfilling (when measured using mAP). However, adding it to <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> to get <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{l_{2}+disc}</annotation></semantics></math> improves results for both random and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> based backfilling for both mAP and CMC-top1.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Ablation on Places-365</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide an ablation study in Figure <a href="#A3.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ Table 6 ‣ C.2 Ablation on Places-365 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> and Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ C.2 Ablation on Places-365 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> on the Places-365 dataset. The conclusion is similar to the ImageNet ablation where FastFill improves its ablations using alternative uncertainty measures and significantly improves previous work FCT.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T6" class="ltx_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure ltx_flex_table">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<figure id="A3.T6.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:318.0pt;">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Table 6: </span>Ablation Study on Places-365: We compare the effect of different training losses and backfilling orderings on the backfilling curves. </figcaption>
<table id="A3.T6.fig1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A3.T6.fig1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A3.T6.fig1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding-bottom: -4.30554pt;"></td>
<td id="A3.T6.fig1.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_top ltx_border_t" style="padding-bottom: -4.30554pt;"></td>
<td id="A3.T6.fig1.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_top ltx_border_t" style="padding-bottom: -4.30554pt;"></td>
<td id="A3.T6.fig1.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_top ltx_border_t" style="padding-bottom: -4.30554pt;"></td>
<td id="A3.T6.fig1.1.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_top ltx_border_t" style="padding-bottom: -4.30554pt;"></td></tr>

</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Ablation on ImageNet-250 to ImageNet-500</h3>

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a further ablation study that compares different evaluation set-ups focusing on different backfilling orderings provide by different uncertainty estimations. We run experiments where the same classes are used during training and evaluation as well as experiments where we evaluate the compatibility on previously unseen classes. The results are illustrated in Figure <a href="#A3.F11" title="Figure 11 ‣ C.3 Ablation on ImageNet-250 to ImageNet-500 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> and Table <a href="#A3.T7.fig1" title="Table 7 ‣ C.3 Ablation on ImageNet-250 to ImageNet-500 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. In every case we train the old model on ImageNet-250 and the new model on ImageNet-500.
For the first set of experiments ([500: ]) we use the first 500 classes for both the query and gallery. This is the <span id="A3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">same train-test classes</span> setup.
For the second experiment ([500:]) we use the second 500 classes for both query and gallery. This is the <span id="A3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">disjoint train-test classes</span> setup.
And finally we use all 1000 classes for both query and gallery ([:1000]). This is a setup where <span id="A3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">half of the train-test classes</span> overlap.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The below results show that Bayesian estimation (FastFill) brings further improved accuracy in the presence of new classes. For example, compared to its ablations, FastFill obtains +1% top-1 improvement when evaluated on the first 500 classes [:500], but gets +2.7% top-1 improvement when evaluated on the second 500 classes [500:] that are unseen during training. Further, when evaluated on unseen classes, ablations of FastFill with logits-based uncertainty estimation gets results close to no uncertainty estimation at all as in FCT.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We note that for most real-world image retrieval tasks (as for instance facial recognition, or zero-shot retrieval) the test-time samples (for gallery and query sets) are coming from new classes that were not present at training-time. Using a training time classification head to measure uncertainty as in RACT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>)</cite> is a major limitation in practice since the relative confidence or entropy between the samples from new classes tend to be not as informative. In contrast, our proposed uncertainty estimation method based on feature alignment is explicitly designed to be class agnostic and works well on previously unseen classes. This is one of our method’s main contributions and novelties.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T7.fig1" class="ltx_table ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:377.6pt;">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Figure 11: </span>Ablation Study on ImageNet: We compare the effect of different training losses and backfilling orderings on the backfilling curves.
<span id="A3.F11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top:</span> [500: ] Use the first 500 classes for both query and gallery. This is the same train-test classes setup.
<span id="A3.F11.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Middle:</span> [500:] Use the second 500 classes for both query and gallery. This is the disjoint train-test classes setup.
<span id="A3.F11.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bottom:</span> [:1000] Use all 1000 classes for both query and gallery. This is a setup where half of the train-test classes overlap.

</section>
<section id="A3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.4 </span>Ablation on VGGFace2</h3>

<div id="A3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We run experiments on VGGFace2 using confidence and entropy based backfilling (as proposed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (30)</a></cite>) on top of our proposed loss for feature alignment and the FCT baseline. We illustrate the results in Figure <a href="#A3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ C.4 Ablation on VGGFace2 ‣ Appendix C Further Ablation Studies ‣ FastFill: Efficient Compatible Model Update" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that entropy/confidence based ablation on top of FastFill and baseline FCT are quite close to random backfilling whereas our proposed uncertainty estimation significantly improves them. Moreover, FastFill variants utilize a transformation function from old to new feature space that leads to significantly improved model update accuracies compared to RACT which directly enforce compatibility between new and old models (more than 5% on top-1 and 25% on mAP metrics).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We note that the uncertainty estimation measures proposed in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (30)</a></cite> (confidence and entropy) are intuitive and simple to use, but rely on the training time classification head. For most real-world image retrieval tasks (e.g. face recognition, or zero-shot retrieval) the test-time samples (for gallery and query sets) are coming from different classes to those seen during training-time. Using the training-time classification head to measure uncertainty as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (30)</a></cite> is a major limitation in practice since the relative confidence/entropy between the samples from new classes tend to be not informative. In contrast, our proposed uncertainty estimation method based on feature alignment is explicitly designed to be class agnostic and works well on previously unseen classes. This is one of our method’s main contributions/novelties.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F12" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Positive and Negative Flips Analysis</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyse the positive and negative flips for FastFill and FCT. A negative flip is an image that gets classified correctly for cross-model retrieval with 0% but gets misclassified when using <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in(0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in(0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> amount of backfilling. Conversely a positive flip is an image that originally gets misclassified but then labelled correctly for some amount of (partial) backfilling. The retrieval performance at a certain backfilling point is a function of the original cross-model retrieval performance at 0% backfilling and plus the number of positive minus the negative flips.
We show FastFill outperforms FCT by both increasing the number of positive flips with limited backfilling whilst also causing fewer negative flips throughout the entire backfilling curve.
We note that even though at 100% backfilling both FCT and FastFill use the same model, the number of flips doesn’t match as it also depends on the cross model performance at 0% backfilling, which is different for the two methods.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.F13" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A4.F13.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/flips_compared_to_0_ImageNet-top1_.png" id="A4.F13.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:548/699;" width="548" height="699" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="A4.F13.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2303.04766v1/plots/flips_compared_to_0_ImageNet-top5_.png" id="A4.F13.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:548/699;" width="548" height="699" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 13: </span>Positive and Negative Flip Analysis on ImageNet. We compare FastFill (blue and orange) and FCT (green and red) on ImageNet using (a) CMC-top1 and (b) top-5 retrieval, respectively. The aim is to maximize the number of positive flips (orange and red), whilst minimizing the number of negative ones (blue and green) with as little backfilling as possible.</figcaption>
</figure>
